_help: Steps for the Future features tour (concept mock-ups at /future-features). Same fields as site_tour_steps.json; every target is a static mock-up element, so nothing here calls the library, an AI or the database.

steps.title: Where iLit could go next
steps.text: This tour walks through concept mock-ups of five future features. None of them is built yet, and every name, number and passage is invented. They show the direction, not what the site does today.

steps.title: Ask in plain words
steps.text: You would type a question the way you would ask a colleague, not a keyword string. The site works today without any AI, and this would be an addition.

steps.title: Passages that mean the same thing
steps.text: Results would be the matching paragraphs, found by meaning rather than exact words. Each says why it matched and links to the source paragraph.

steps.title: Runs on the agency's computer
steps.text: Paragraph fingerprints would be made when a decision is added, and your question would be handled on the same computer. Nothing is sent to an outside AI service.

steps.title: Not just who cites a case, but how
steps.text: For a case you are about to rely on, this would show how later decisions treated it: followed, applied, distinguished, questioned or criticised.

steps.title: A plain-language line for each citing case
steps.text: Each citing case would get a one-sentence summary of what it did with the authority, with a link to the exact paragraph so you can check it.

steps.title: A warning when the tide turns
steps.text: Treatment over time would flag an authority whose recent citations are drifting from "followed" to "distinguished". The labels would be written at ingest and stored as data.

steps.title: One search, two sources
steps.text: An agency copy could search the public library and the agency's own records together, with a clear switch for each. Private records are marked so they are never confused with public ones.

steps.title: Private decisions next to public ones
steps.text: Results could include Immigration Division decisions and internal notes beside Federal Court cases, each labelled by source. The records shown here are invented.

steps.title: Kept on the agency's network
steps.text: Public decisions would flow in one way. Private records stay behind the agency's sign-in and are never copied to the public site.

steps.title: Find the arguments in a memorandum
steps.text: The tool would list each argument in a filed memorandum, and show which ones the other side has already answered.

steps.title: Spot the argument still open
steps.text: An argument with no answer yet is highlighted, so it is the first thing you see rather than something you find on the fourth read.

steps.title: A case to cite in reply
steps.text: For an open argument, the tool would suggest a case that answers it, with the passage, the reason, and how later cases have treated it. A person decides what to file.

steps.title: Teamwork and alerts
steps.text: The Workbench could grow into shared folders and notes for a team, and saved searches could send a short weekly list of new decisions.

steps.title: People and tribunals
steps.text: Judge and decision-maker insights would show the number of cases behind every figure. Immigration Division and Appeal Division decisions would need an agency data feed.

steps.title: One rule for all of it
steps.text: Normal search keeps working with no AI. Any AI would run when decisions are added, or on the agency's own computer, and its output is stored as data you can check. That is the end of the tour.
